title: Faithful or Fabricated

post.author: u/night_adjuster_tryphena
post.title: I'm the night claims adjuster at a home insurer. Our assistant's answers would pass a polygraph. Tonight one quoted a section of a document that doesn't exist.

blocks.text: I'm Tryphena, the night claims adjuster at Wyvernhold Home Insurance. An adjuster decides whether a policy pays for damage, and how much. My desk is in the old interview room, where the fraud team once ran polygraph tests: a machine that watches a person's pulse and breathing for the signs of a lie. It still sits in the cupboard.
Every policy is three kinds of paper. The wording is the long booklet everyone gets, in numbered sections. The schedule is one page of your own details.
An endorsement is a separate one-page document that changes the wording for some customers, such as everyone in one postcode. An endorsement that takes cover away is an exclusion.

Since spring, customers' questions go first to a drafting assistant, in two steps. First, a search reads through our documents, cut into short pieces called passages, and ranks them against the question. The best four are kept. That finding step is called retrieval.

Then a language model, a program that writes text one likely word at a time, writes an answer from those four passages. I read each draft before it goes out. They read beautifully: calm, specific, never a pause. My private name for it: it would pass a polygraph.
Tonight Mr Gwinnett, in Steadfold by the river, asked about flood. Each line below shows the time, who wrote, and what they wrote.

01:52  customer  Does my policy cover flood damage?
01:52  draft     Yes. Your policy covers flood damage. Cover is up to
                 £25,000. This is set out in section 4.2 of your Flood
                 Cover Addendum.

Section 4.2 of the wording does cover flood. It names no £25,000. There is no Flood Cover Addendum; we have never written one. And Mr Gwinnett's schedule lists Endorsement 17, which deletes section 4.2 for his postcode. I looked at the passages the search had ranked. Section 4.2 came first. Endorsement 17 came sixth, two places below the four the model read.
A clause, a section number, a sum. Everything a true answer has, except a page it came from.

Mr Sutterby runs the assistant. His screen shows one score, answer relevance: a tool rates whether each answer is about what was asked, from 0 to 1, and averages the ratings. It reads 0.94. Mr Gwinnett's answer scored 0.97.
The vendor also sells an automated faithfulness check, a second model that splits each answer into claims, single things it says, and looks for each one in the passages. Nobody switched it on.

In spring I wrote the team a labelled set: real customer questions, each with the passages that hold its answer and the claims a correct answer makes. Nobody used it. Tonight I added Mr Gwinnett's question as the tenth. Mr Sutterby says 0.94 is excellent, and from next month he wants drafts to go straight to customers, without me. What should I ask for first?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that room is haunted, not even the cupboard. Your assistant is RAG, retrieval-augmented generation: look things up, then write from what was found. The trade has words for how well each step did. Context precision: of the passages retrieved, the share your labels call relevant, meaning they hold part of the answer. Context recall: of the claims a correct answer makes, the share the retrieved passages hold. Faithfulness, from Season 3: the share of an answer's own claims that its passages support. And answer relevance asks only whether the answer is about the question; a false answer can score near 1. Two questions. Which of tonight's three claims can you find in the four passages the model read? And why would the search rank Endorsement 17 sixth for a question about flood?

replies.author: u/night_adjuster_tryphena
replies.text: Only the first: section 4.2 says flood is covered. The £25,000 and the Addendum are in none of the four, or anywhere else we keep. Why sixth, I don't know. I'll ask the clerk who files the endorsements.

comments.author: u/on_topic_kersey
comments.text: I run quality for a bank's chatbot. Answer relevance of 0.94 is excellent; most teams would be glad of it. Every answer is on topic. This is one bad answer, not a measurement problem, and you're about to bury a working assistant under spreadsheets. Fix the answer instead: add a line to the prompt, the standing instructions the model gets with every question, telling it to answer only from the documents provided. Models follow instructions. Then let it run.

replies.author: u/night_adjuster_tryphena
replies.text: Mr Gwinnett's answer was very much on topic.

comments.author: u/endorsement_desk_venning
comments.text: Underwriting clerk here; I write and file the endorsements. Each one is a single page, filed apart from the wording, and a schedule lists them by number only: Endorsements: 17. Endorsement 17 never uses the word flood. It says section 4.2 is deleted for the postcodes below, then a list of postcodes, Steadfold's among them. A search looking for passages about flood has very little in it to find. There are plenty more like it in the drawer.

reply.prompt: From next month, Mr Sutterby wants drafts to go to customers without an adjuster. What should Tryphena ask for first? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Score labelled questions on whether retrieval found the clause and the answer kept to it.
options.part2: I scored the 10 labelled questions as tonight's drafts stand, four passages each. Answer relevance 0.94. Context precision 0.35, context recall 0.90, faithfulness 0.83. Three questions failed. Mr Gwinnett's: context recall 0.50, because Endorsement 17 was sixth, and faithfulness 0.33, one claim of three. The laptop question, Q4: context recall 0.50 with the customer's schedule fifth, and a cover claim section 6.2 doesn't make. The bike, Q9: a £1,000 limit from no passage. Before trusting a machine with my labelling, I ran the automated faithfulness check on the same 20 claims. Its average was 0.83 too, yet it agreed with me on only 18 of 20: it passed the laptop claim and failed a true one on Q7. Mr Sutterby kept me on the drafts. The scorecard now runs on every change, with a bar for context recall and faithfulness, and the check never clears a cover claim alone.
options.senior: Grade the two steps of a RAG system apart, on labelled questions. Context recall asks whether retrieval found everything the answer needed; faithfulness asks whether the answer kept to what was found. Answer relevance only says the answer is on topic. Then check any automated scorer against a person's labels claim by claim, because an equal average can hide opposite mistakes.

options.text: Add 'answer only from the documents provided' to the prompt, and trust the answers after.
options.part2: We added the line. On my 10 labelled questions, faithfulness rose from 0.83 to 0.90. Mr Gwinnett's draft lost the £25,000 and the Addendum, and now reads: Your policy covers flood damage. Faithfulness 1.00, every word in a passage, and still wrong. The search still ranked Endorsement 17 sixth, so context recall for his question stayed 0.50. The bike answer kept its £1,000 limit anyway. Mr Sutterby called it fixed.
options.senior: A prompt line can help answers keep to their passages, and it is worth having, but it can't put back a passage retrieval never found. A faithful answer is only as right as what was retrieved. And without a score before and after, nobody knows whether the line worked: here it fixed one draft and missed another.

options.text: Have a second model rate each answer's confidence, and send the low ones to an adjuster.
options.verdict: Sounding sure is not a check
options.part2: A second model rated each draft's confidence, and anything below 0.70 came to me. Of the 10 labelled questions, one did: the bike, at 0.64. Mr Gwinnett's flood answer rated 0.93, the laptop answer 0.88. Of the three drafts I had marked wrong, two would have gone straight to customers. Confident is how the drafts always sound. It is why I named it for a polygraph.
options.senior: Confidence measures how sure an answer sounds, not whether the documents back it, and made-up clauses usually read as calmly as true ones. Send answers to a person on a measure tied to the documents, such as whether every claim rests on a passage, and check that measure against a person's labels first.

options.text: Retrieve twice as many passages for every question, so the exclusion is more likely found.
options.part2: We raised the search from four passages to eight. For Mr Gwinnett's question, Endorsement 17 came in, sixth. On my 10 labelled questions, context recall rose from 0.90 to 1.00 and context precision fell from 0.35 to 0.20: four in five passages the model now reads hold nothing it needs. Did the drafts use the endorsement? Nobody knew, because nobody had scored the answers, and the £25,000 sits in no passage at any depth. I asked to score them before the next change.
options.senior: Retrieving more can raise context recall, and here it found the endorsement. But it lowers context precision, costs more to read, and gives the model more to get wrong. Whether it helps is a measured question: score retrieval and the answers on labelled questions, before and after.

sim.title: Score the drafting assistant on the labelled set
sim.lede: You're Tryphena at the night desk, the night Mr Gwinnett asked about flood. The scorecard holds your labelled set: 10 customer questions, Q1 to Q10. For each you marked the passages that hold the answer (relevant) and the claims a correct answer makes. The search's ranking of 8 passages per question, tonight's drafts written from the top 4, each draft split into claims, and three cosine scores per answer are stated data, not a real model. Context precision at k is relevant passages in the top k divided by k. Context recall at k is a correct answer's claims whose passage is in the top k, divided by all of them. Faithfulness is the draft's supported claims divided by its claims; the drafts don't change with k. Answer relevance is the mean of three cosine scores (closeness of meaning, 0 to 1), each comparing the real question with a question the answer looks like it is answering. Every score is the plain mean over the 10. The prompt line drops Q1's two claims that rest on no passage, and nothing else. You can switch whose labels judge the claims: yours, or the automated faithfulness check's.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you open on tonight at k 4: answer relevance 0.94, context precision 0.35, context recall 0.90, faithfulness 0.83, and Q1 at 0.50 recall and 0.33 faithfulness. Pick context recall on Q1: Endorsement 17 is 6th, missed. Slide k to 8: recall 1.00, precision 0.20, faithfulness unchanged. Back at 4, switch the prompt line on: faithfulness 0.90 and Q1 1.00, recall still 0.50. Then judge the claims by the automated check: still 0.83 overall, but open Q4 and Q7. Last, try each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the assistant lied on purpose. Retrieval left out the one page that removed flood cover, and the model wrote a confident answer from what it had, adding a sum and a document from nowhere. The only score measured whether answers were on topic. The case needed retrieval and the answer graded apart, on labelled questions.

steps.title: Two steps, each able to fail on its own.
steps.text: The drafting assistant is RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, from a3e01: look up passages, then write from them. It works in steps. First, the question is compared with every passage and the passages are ranked. Second, the top 4 are handed to the language model with the question. Third, the model writes an answer from them. Each step can fail. Retrieval can leave out a passage the answer needs, as it left out Endorsement 17. The model can write things no passage says, as it wrote £25,000. Or it can stay true to passages that were never the whole story. a5e02 scored the first step alone, by which documents came back. This case scores both steps, and the answer's link to the question, on one labelled set. Es et al. call the three qualities faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance, often called the RAG triad; the RAGAS library adds context precision and context recall.

steps.title: Context precision and context recall: did retrieval bring the right pages?
steps.text: Both are worked out from Tryphena's labels in steps. First, take the passages the search kept, the top k. Second, mark which ones she labelled relevant. Third, for context precision, divide the relevant ones by k. For Q1 at k = 4, only Wording 4.2 is relevant: 1 / 4 = 0.25. Fourth, for context recall, take the claims a correct answer makes, each tied to the passage that holds it, and divide those whose passage was kept by all of them. Q1's correct answer makes two: the wording covers flood (Wording 4.2, kept) and Endorsement 17 removes it (sixth, not kept). 1 / 2 = 0.50. Over the 10 questions, context precision is 0.35 and context recall 0.90. Only Q1 and Q4 lose recall, and both lost the passage that limits the cover: the endorsement, and the customer's schedule. What can go wrong: a passage nobody labelled counts as irrelevant, so the scores are only as good as the labels. Raising k to 8 lifts recall to 1.00 and drops precision to 0.20.

steps.title: Faithfulness: split the answer, then check each claim.
steps.text: a3e06 defined faithfulness: supported claims divided by all claims, measured over a set of questions. The steps: first, split the answer into claims, one thing each. Second, for each claim, look for a passage the model was given that says it. Third, divide the supported claims by all of them. Tonight's draft makes three. Your policy covers flood damage: Wording 4.2 says so, supported. Cover is up to £25,000: in no passage. Section 4.2 of your Flood Cover Addendum: no such document. 1 / 3 = 0.33. Over the 10, faithfulness is 0.83; Q4 and Q9 are 0.50 each. Now the trap. With the prompt line on, the draft drops its two unsupported claims and says only that flood is covered. Faithfulness for Q1 becomes 1.00, and the answer is still wrong, because the passage that removes the cover was never retrieved. Faithfulness checks the answer against what was found, never against what should have been found. That is context recall's job.

steps.title: Answer relevance: on topic, not true.
steps.text: Es et al. measure answer relevance in steps. First, a language model reads the answer and writes a few questions it looks like it is answering. Second, each of those questions and the real question are turned into embeddings, lists of numbers for their meaning (a1e04). Third, the closeness of each pair is measured by cosine similarity, near 1 for the same meaning. Last, the scores are averaged. For Q1 the sim states three: (0.98 + 0.96 + 0.97) / 3 = 0.97. The draft is plainly about flood cover, so it scores high. Answer relevance catches answers that wander or dodge the question. It cannot see whether a single claim is true, which is why 0.94 overall sat beside three wrong drafts.

steps.title: Calibrating the automated check against a person.
steps.text: Calibrating a measure means checking it against a trusted one before you rely on it. The steps: first, run the automated faithfulness check and the person on the same claims. Second, compare them claim by claim, not just their averages. Third, read every disagreement and note which way it went. Fourth, decide where the check can be trusted alone, and run the comparison again whenever the check or its model changes. Here the check and Tryphena agree on 18 of 20 claims, and both average 0.83. The two disagreements cancel. On Q4 the check passed a claim she failed: section 6.2 covers accidental damage only if the schedule shows it, and the model said the laptop was covered. That is the dangerous direction, a false pass on a cover claim. On Q7 it failed a true claim, reading empty as different from unoccupied. A false fail costs an adjuster a minute; a false pass reaches a customer.

diagram.aria: The scorecard. The labelled set of 10 questions feeds both steps. Retrieval at k 4: context precision 0.35, context recall 0.90; for Q1, the flood question, recall 0.50 with Endorsement 17 sixth. The drafted answers: faithfulness 0.83 and answer relevance 0.94; for Q1, faithfulness 0.33 and relevance 0.97. The automated check agrees with the adjuster on 18 of 20 claims.

notes.text: the check agrees with the adjuster on 18 of 20 claims

explain.caption: Read left to right. The same 10 labelled questions score both steps. Retrieval: context precision 0.35, context recall 0.90, with Q1 at 0.50 because Endorsement 17 ranked sixth. The answers: faithfulness 0.83 and answer relevance 0.94, with Q1 at 0.33 and 0.97. The automated check agrees with the adjuster on 18 of 20 claims.

fix.title: The fix: score both steps on labelled questions, and calibrate the check
fix.text: Keep the labelled set and grow it: every draft an adjuster corrects becomes a new question, with its relevant passages and its correct-answer claims. Report four scores on every change, overall and per question: context precision, context recall, faithfulness and answer relevance. Agree pass bars in advance, such as context recall and faithfulness of 1.00 on every question about what a policy covers, and keep an adjuster on the drafts until the scorecard clears them. Fix the retrieval gap the scorecard found: when a customer's schedule lists an endorsement, always hand that endorsement to the model with the question. Before the automated check scores anything alone, compare it with the adjuster's labels claim by claim, look at each disagreement, and repeat the comparison whenever the check or its model changes. Where it falsely passes cover claims, a person reads those claims.

limits: Ten questions is a small set: one question moves an average by a tenth. Read every failing question, not just the means, and grow the set with every corrected draft.
The labels come from one adjuster. A relevant passage she missed counts against precision, and a claim she misjudged counts against faithfulness. Have a second adjuster label a sample.
Twenty claims is a small calibration, and it holds only for the check and model it was run on. Faithfulness also can't say whether a true answer is complete or clear to the customer.

explain.seniorTake: A RAG system fails in two places, so measure it in two places. Context recall and precision tell you whether retrieval brought the right pages; faithfulness tells you whether the answer kept to them; answer relevance tells you only that it stayed on topic. Measure all of them on labelled questions, read the failures one by one, and never let one good average stand for the rest. Before an automated scorer replaces a person, compare the two claim by claim, because equal averages can hide opposite mistakes.

realWorld.title: Es et al., 2023: three qualities of a RAG answer
realWorld.text: Shahul Es, Jithin James, Luis Espinosa-Anke and Steven Schockaert's paper introduces Ragas, a framework for reference-free evaluation, meaning it scores answers without a correct answer written in advance. It names three qualities. Faithfulness refers to the idea that the answer should be grounded in the given context. Answer relevance refers to the idea that the generated answer should address the actual question. Context relevance refers to the idea that the retrieved context should be focused, since long passages cost more and are harder for a model to use.

realWorld.title: How the paper scores faithfulness and answer relevance
realWorld.text: For faithfulness, an answer is faithful when the claims that are made in the answer can be inferred from the context. The paper first uses an LLM, a large language model, to extract a set of statements from the answer, checks each against the context, and divides the statements supported by all of them. For answer relevance, an answer counts when it directly addresses the question in an appropriate way: the model generates n potential questions from the answer, and the score is the mean cosine similarity between their embeddings and the real question's.

realWorld.title: Agreement with people, and the hardest quality
realWorld.text: The paper tests its scores against human annotators on its WikiEval dataset, counting how often the answer or context the method prefers matches the one people preferred. Ragas agrees 0.95 of the time on faithfulness, 0.78 on answer relevance and 0.70 on context relevance. The authors write: We found context relevance to be the hardest quality dimension to evaluate. That is a calibration against people, on their data; it says nothing about how a check will do on insurance wordings until you run it on yours.

realWorld.title: Context precision, in the RAGAS documentation
realWorld.text: The RAGAS library's documentation says context precision is a metric that evaluates the retriever's ability to rank relevant chunks higher than irrelevant ones. It defines Precision@k as true positives@k divided by true positives@k plus false positives@k, the share relevant among the top k, and averages that over the ranks where a relevant chunk sits. This case uses the plain share at k; the library's form also rewards putting relevant passages first.

realWorld.title: Context recall, in the RAGAS documentation
realWorld.text: The documentation says context recall measures how many of the relevant documents (or pieces of information) were successfully retrieved. Its score is the number of claims in the reference answer supported by the retrieved context, divided by the total number of claims in the reference. Each claim is analyzed to determine whether it can be attributed to the retrieved context or not, and in an ideal scenario, all claims in the reference answer should be attributable to the retrieved context.

asked: How do you evaluate a RAG system end to end?
How would you know your automated metric is right?
interview.answer: Evaluate the two steps apart, then together. Build a labelled set: real questions, each with the passages that hold its answer and the claims a correct answer makes, a few dozen to start, grown with every failure found. For retrieval, score context recall, the share of a correct answer's claims the retrieved passages hold, and context precision, the share of retrieved passages that are relevant, at the k you really use. For the answer, score faithfulness: split it into claims, check each against the passages it was given, and divide supported by all. Add answer relevance to catch answers that wander, knowing it says nothing about truth. Read the failing questions one by one, because a faithful answer can still be wrong when retrieval missed a page, like a policy exclusion. Then the automated metric: before trusting it, run it and a person on the same claims, compare claim by claim, and read each disagreement and its direction. A false pass on a high-stakes claim matters more than a false fail. Equal averages prove nothing, since opposite errors cancel. Repeat the comparison whenever the scorer or its model changes, and gate releases on agreed bars.

terms.def: The person at an insurer who decides whether a policy pays for damage, and how much. Tryphena is Wyvernhold's night adjuster and reads each draft before it goes out.
A machine that records pulse, breathing and sweating while someone answers questions, to look for signs of a lie. Tryphena's desk is in the room where the fraud team once used one.
An insurance contract: what the insurer will pay for, up to what amounts, and what it won't. A home policy here is three kinds of paper: wording, schedule, endorsements.
The long booklet every customer gets, in numbered sections, such as section 4.2 on flood. Endorsements can change it for some customers.
One page of a customer's own details: their excess, the optional covers they bought, and the endorsements that apply, listed by number only.
A separate one-page document that changes the wording for some customers. Endorsement 17 deletes section 4.2, flood, for a list of postcodes, Steadfold's among them.
Wording that takes cover away. Endorsement 17 is one: it removes flood cover where the river floods.
The part of each claim the customer pays first, before the insurer pays the rest. Q3's customer pays £250; for subsidence it is £1,000.
The ground under a house sinking, which can crack walls. Section 4.5 of Wyvernhold's wording covers it.
The insurers' name for damage from a burst or leaking pipe. Section 3.1 covers it, unless the home was unoccupied more than 60 days in a row.
A person in an insurer's underwriting team, which decides what to cover and on what terms. Venning writes and files the endorsements.
Wyvernhold's RAG system: it finds the four passages that best match a customer's question and has a language model write an answer from them, for an adjuster to check.
The finding step: comparing the question with every passage, ranking them, and keeping the best few to hand to the model. Wyvernhold keeps four.
A passage Tryphena labelled as holding part of a question's answer. Q1's are Wording 4.2 and Endorsement 17.
Questions with the right answers marked in advance by a person, kept to score every version: a golden set. Tryphena's has 10, each with relevant passages and a correct answer's claims.
The correct answer written by a person for a labelled question, split into claims. The RAGAS documentation calls it the reference. Q1's makes two claims.
Of the passages retrieved for a question, the share labelled relevant. Q1 at k 4: 1 of 4, 0.25. The RAGAS library's version also rewards putting relevant passages first.
Of the claims a correct answer makes, the share whose passage was retrieved. Q1: 1 of 2, 0.50, because Endorsement 17 ranked sixth.
The share of an answer's claims the source supports: supported claims divided by all claims, measured over a set of questions. Defined in a3e06; Q1 tonight is 1 of 3.
How closely an answer addresses the question asked, from 0 to 1. Es et al. score it from questions generated from the answer. It says nothing about truth: Q1 scores 0.97.
Es et al.'s third quality: the retrieved passages should be focused, holding what the question needs and little else. Context precision is the library's nearest measure.
A common name for the three qualities Es et al. score: faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance, one each for the answer, the question and the passages.
A second model that splits each answer into claims and checks each against the passages, so faithfulness can be scored without a person. It needs checking against a person first.
Checking a measure against a trusted one, here a person's labels, claim by claim, before relying on it, and again whenever it changes. Like checking a new scale against known weights.
A false pass is a check calling an unsupported claim supported, as on Q4's laptop. A false fail calls a supported claim unsupported, as on Q7.
The share of items on which two graders give the same verdict. The automated check and Tryphena agree on 18 of 20 claims.
A closeness score between two embeddings, lists of numbers for meaning: near 1 for the same meaning, near 0 for unrelated (a1e04). Answer relevance averages it.
In Es et al.'s answer relevance, a question a model writes from the answer alone: what this answer looks like it is answering. The sim states three for each answer.
A sentence added to the model's standing instructions, here: answer only from the documents provided. In the sim it drops Q1's two unsupported claims and nothing else.
A score from a second model for how sure an answer seems, 0 to 1. Option C sends anything below 0.70 to an adjuster. Q1 rates 0.93.
What Ragas calls a claim: one short assertion split out of an answer, checked against the context.
Short for large language model: a language model trained on a very large amount of text, of the kind the drafting assistant uses.
Scoring answers without a correct answer written in advance, as Ragas's faithfulness and answer relevance do. Context recall, by contrast, needs a reference answer.
The small dataset Es et al. built from Wikipedia pages, with human judgments, to test how often Ragas agrees with people.
In the RAGAS documentation, true positives at k divided by true positives plus false positives at k: the share of the top k that is relevant.
The score a change must reach before it ships, agreed in advance, such as context recall of 1.00 on every cover question.
A program that runs a system on a labelled set and works out the scores, the same way every time. Build Night X2 builds one for the Nightwatch copilot.
The international standard for quality management. Clause 9.1 covers deciding what to monitor and measure; clause 8.5.1 covers providing a service under controlled conditions.

atWork: Look for an assistant at work that answers from rules: an HR assistant quoting the staff handbook, a policy assistant quoting procedures, a support bot quoting terms. A common pattern: it reads well, everyone likes it, and one day it quotes a rule with a section number that no document holds, or misses the one page that changes the rule for some people. Ask four things. Is there a labelled set of real questions, with the passages that hold each answer and the claims a correct answer makes? Is retrieval scored on its own, context recall above all, so a missed exception shows up? Is every answer split into claims and checked against the passages it was given? And if a model does that checking, has anyone compared it with a person, claim by claim, since the last time it changed? Build Night X2, after a5e04, builds an eval harness for the Nightwatch copilot; this scorecard is its answer-quality half, run on every change. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO 9001:2015, the international standard for quality management, or working toward it, clause 9.1 (monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation) covers deciding what to measure, how and when, and evaluating the results, and clause 8.5.1 covers providing a service under controlled conditions, which includes suitable monitoring and measurement at the right stages. A scorecard run on every change, an automated check with its calibration kept, and a person on high-stakes answers until the bars are met is the kind of evidence both look for, and far cheaper built in from the first version than gathered before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your company's HR assistant answers staff questions from the staff handbook: it searches the handbook, then a language model writes the answer. The team tracks one score, how on topic the answers are, at 0.92. Last week it told a manager that staff get ten days of compassionate leave under section 7.3, and no page of the handbook says so. What do you set up before anyone trusts it again?

keyIdeas.idea: Build a labelled set: real questions, each with the passages that hold the answer and the claims a correct answer makes
Score retrieval on its own: context recall, whether the search brought back every passage the answer needs, and context precision
Split each answer into claims and check every claim against the passages it was given: faithfulness
Before trusting an automated check, compare it with a person's labels claim by claim

recall.model: I'd build a labelled set first: real questions from staff, each with the handbook passages that hold the answer and the claims a correct answer makes, marked in advance by someone in HR. Then I'd score the two steps apart. For retrieval, context recall, whether the search brought back every passage the answer needs, and context precision. For the answer, faithfulness: split the answer into claims and check each claim against the passages it was given; ten days under section 7.3 would show up as a claim with no passage. The on-topic score stays, but it can't see truth. If a model does the claim checking, I'd calibrate it first, comparing it with a person's labels claim by claim and reading every disagreement.

recall.prompt: A correct answer makes 3 claims, and the retrieved passages hold 2 of them. The drafted answer makes 4 claims, and the passages support 3. What are context recall and faithfulness, in that order?
recall.why: Context recall divides the correct answer's claims the passages hold, 2, by all of them, 3: 0.67. Faithfulness divides the draft's supported claims, 3, by its claims, 4: 0.75. Swapping the two gives 0.75 and 0.67.

recall.prompt: A teammate says: the automated faithfulness check scores our 10 questions at 0.83, exactly what the adjuster's labels give, so we can stop paying for the adjuster's time. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: Equal averages can hide disagreements that cancel out; compare the two claim by claim
Count where they agree and read each disagreement, noting which way it went
A false pass on a high-stakes claim is the dangerous error; keep a person on those and re-check whenever the check changes

recall.model: An equal average proves little, because opposite mistakes cancel. I'd compare the two claim by claim. Count where they agree, then read each disagreement and which way it went. On our set they disagree on two claims: the check passes Q4's laptop claim, which the policy doesn't support, and fails a true claim on Q7. That first one is a false pass on a claim about what a policy covers, the error that reaches a customer. So the check can't clear cover claims alone yet: keep a person on those, and re-check the comparison whenever the check or its model changes.

recall.prompt: A draft says only: Your policy covers flood damage. Every word is in a retrieved passage, but the search missed the one-page document that removes flood cover for this customer. Which measure catches the problem?
options: The share of the draft's claims its passages support
How closely the draft addresses the question
The share of a correct answer's claims the retrieved passages hold
recall.why: Context recall asks whether the passages a correct answer needs were retrieved; the exclusion wasn't, so it falls to 0.50. Faithfulness only checks the draft against what was retrieved, so it scores 1.00. Answer relevance sees an on-topic answer, and confidence sees a calm one.

recall.prompt: An answer scores 0.97 on answer relevance. What does that tell you?
options: Its claims all rest on the passages it was given
It addresses the question that was asked, true or not
Every passage the answer needed was in the top results
A person checked it and found it correct
recall.why: Answer relevance compares questions generated from the answer with the real question, so it measures whether the answer is about the question. It never checks a claim against a passage, so a fabricated answer can score 0.97, as Mr Gwinnett's did.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 6 months later. The scorecard runs every time the assistant changes, and the automated check now clears most drafts, after we compared it with my labels in spring. Endorsements on a customer's schedule always go to the model now. In September the vendor quietly moved the check to a newer model. Nobody compared it with my labels again. Since then, faithfulness has read between 0.97 and 0.99 every week, the best it has ever been. Tonight a draft told a customer their contents were covered up to £60,000 under Endorsement 22. We have never had an Endorsement 22. The check marked it supported.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did faithfulness rise while a made-up clause went through, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The check changed when its model changed, so the spring calibration no longer holds; the rise may be the check passing more, not the answers improving
Compare the check with the adjuster's labels again, claim by claim, and read the false passes
Make the comparison a gate: re-run it whenever the check or its model changes, with a bar on agreement, and keep a person on cover claims until it passes

coldCase.model: The answers didn't get better; the grader changed. The spring calibration was for the old check, and a new model behind it no longer holds to it. A score that jumps to its best ever just after the scorer changed is more likely the check passing more than the drafts improving, and tonight's Endorsement 22 is a false pass on a cover claim. I'd compare it with the adjuster's labels again, claim by claim, on the labelled set, and read every false pass. Then I'd make that comparison a gate: whenever the check or its model changes, it is re-run, with a bar on agreement, before the check's scores count. Until it passes, a person reads every cover claim, and Endorsement 22 joins the labelled set.
